title: The Great Bazaar Mystery: Why Rs.100 Buys Less Today
hook: Ravi's grandmother remembers buying a full lunch for Rs.20. Today it costs Rs.200. What happened to money?

slides.title: Ravi Asks Nani a Question
slides.storyContext: Ravi comes home excited - his friend Arun got Rs.500 pocket money while he only got Rs.400. He complains it's unfair. Nani smiles and says, "Beta, when I was your age, Rs.100 could buy lunch, a drink, and sweets. Last week I spent Rs.200 for the same meal. That's not Arun's luck - that's inflation." Ravi is confused. "What is inflation, Nani?"

image.alt: Ravi Asks Nani a Question — Inflation - Why Prices Rise Over Time

slides.title: What Is Inflation?
slides.storyContext: Nani takes Ravi to Mr. Patel's grocery shop. She shows him the price board: "Rice was Rs.40/kg last year. Today it's Rs.50/kg. Vegetables went from Rs.20 to Rs.25. Even milk rose from Rs.50 to Rs.60 a liter." Ravi notices every price went UP. Nani explains: "This is inflation - it means prices of things we buy rise over time."

points.label: Definition
points.text: Inflation is a general, sustained increase in the average price level of goods and services in an economy over time.

points.label: Key idea
points.text: When inflation happens, the same Rs.100 note buys you LESS than before because prices have gone up.

points.label: Real-life impact
points.text: Your pocket money or salary stays the same, but it feels like you're getting poorer - you can buy fewer things.

example.problem: In 2010, a samosa cost Rs.5. In 2026, the same samosa costs Rs.15. What happened?
example.solution: Prices tripled due to inflation. The purchasing power of Rs.1 decreased. You now need Rs.15 instead of Rs.5 for one samosa. This is inflation in action.

slides.inSimpleWords: Inflation means the prices of everyday things keep going up, so your money buys less over time.

image.alt: What Is Inflation? — Inflation - Why Prices Rise Over Time

slides.title: The Rupee's Shrinking Power
slides.storyContext: Ravi asks: "But Nani, my Rs.100 note is still Rs.100. What do you mean it buys less?" Nani pulls out an old photo. "Look - in 1990, I could buy a whole meal, tea, and dessert for Rs.30. Today, the same meal costs Rs.150. The Rs.30 note is still Rs.30, but what it CAN BUY has shrunk. That's the invisible force of inflation eating your money's power." Ravi starts to understand..

slides.title: Purchasing Power vs. Nominal Value
slides.storyContext: Mr. Patel explains while Ravi watches him stock shelves: "Nominal value is the number on the note - Rs.100 is Rs.100. But purchasing power is what it ACTUALLY buys. In 2000, Rs.100 bought me 10 notebooks. Today, Rs.100 buys me only 2 notebooks. Same note, way less buying power. Inflation steals this silently."

points.label: Nominal value
points.text: The number written on money: Rs.100 is always Rs.100 regardless of time or inflation.

points.label: Purchasing power
points.text: What that money can actually buy. Inflation reduces purchasing power - same Rs.100 buys fewer goods over time.

points.label: Real vs. nominal
points.text: Nominal: the face value. Real: adjusted for inflation. Real is what matters for your wealth.

example.problem: In 2015, Rs.1,000 could buy 50 notebooks at Rs.20 each. In 2026, notebooks cost Rs.50 each. What is the purchasing power change?
example.solution: 2015: Rs.1,000 buys 50 notebooks. 2026: same Rs.1,000 buys only 20 notebooks. Purchasing power fell from 50 units to 20 units - a 60% loss in real terms.

slides.inSimpleWords: The number on your money stays same; what it buys shrinks. That shrinkage is inflation's real damage.

slides.title: Inflation Calculation: Quick Practice
slides.storyContext: Ravi asks, "How do we measure inflation?" Nani shows him: "Take a simple item - a pen. In 2024, it cost Rs.10. In 2026, it costs Rs.11. Inflation = (11-10)/10 = 0.1 = 10% per year. Easy, right?"

points.label: Formula
points.text: Inflation rate = (New Price - Old Price) / Old Price x 100

points.label: Interpretation
points.text: 10% inflation means prices rose 10% on average.

example.problem: A notebook cost Rs.20 last year, now Rs.22. Calculate inflation.

slides.inSimpleWords: To find inflation: subtract old price from new price, divide by old price, multiply by 100.

slides.title: Ravi's Snack Diary Discovery
slides.storyContext: Ravi decides to track his favorite snack - a chocolate bar. He digs through his diary: 6 months ago, Rs.20. 3 months ago, Rs.22. Today, Rs.25. "Nani, this chocolate got 25% more expensive in just 6 months!" Nani nods: "Notice how EVERY item goes up? That's inflation - not a one-time jump, but a continuous creep that compounds over years."

slides.title: Why Do Prices Rise?
slides.storyContext: Ravi asks, "But WHY do prices go up, Nani?" Nani explains: "Three big reasons. One: when the government prints more money, there's too much money chasing the same amount of goods - prices rise. Two: production costs go up - farmers need more for seeds and labor, so vegetables cost more. Three: people demand more, but there's limited supply - like when monsoon ruins crops, tomato prices jump."

points.label: More money in economy
points.text: If the government prints more currency and people have more cash, prices rise because demand exceeds supply.

points.label: Production costs increase
points.text: If labor, electricity, fuel, and raw materials become expensive, businesses charge more to maintain profit.

points.label: Supply shocks
points.text: Bad weather, poor harvest, or shortage of goods can make prices spike (e.g., onion crisis in India, 2019-2020).

example.problem: During monsoon, tomato farmers lose 30% of crops. Demand stays high but supply drops. What happens to tomato prices?
example.solution: Tomato prices rise sharply. Fewer tomatoes available + same demand = higher price. This is a supply shock causing inflation for that item.

slides.inSimpleWords: Prices go up when there's too much money, production costs rise, or there aren't enough goods to go around.

image.alt: Why Do Prices Rise? — Inflation - Why Prices Rise Over Time

slides.title: The Onion Crisis That Taught Ravi
slides.storyContext: Ravi's mom mentions the 2019 onion crisis: "Onions went from Rs.10/kg to Rs.80/kg overnight!" Ravi learns: "But that was temporary - a supply shock. Once harvests came back, prices fell again." Nani clarifies: "That was deflation in action - temporary. But GENERAL inflation, like what we see year after year averaging 5-6%, is persistent. That's the real thief of your money over decades."

slides.title: The Bazaar Price Comparison
slides.storyContext: Ravi becomes detective and compares prices with Nani from her old shopping lists. She finds a receipt from 1990: onions Rs.3/kg, milk Rs.12/liter, bread Rs.2 a loaf. Today: onions Rs.25/kg, milk Rs.60/liter, bread Rs.20 a loaf. "See how much everything jumped?" Nani points. "This happened slowly over 35 years. Each year, a little bit of inflation. Add them all up, and wow!" Ravi realizes inflation is cumulative.

image.alt: The Bazaar Price Comparison — Inflation - Why Prices Rise Over Time

slides.title: Compound Effect of Inflation Over Time
slides.storyContext: Ravi calculates: if something costs Rs.100 and inflation is 5% per year, in 10 years it costs Rs.100 x (1.05)^10 = Rs.162.89. In 20 years, Rs.265.33! "So even small yearly inflation adds up MASSIVELY?" Nani nods: "That's why we call inflation the silent killer of savings. It sneaks up on you."

points.label: Compound inflation
points.text: Each year's inflation builds on the previous. 5% in year 1 + 5% in year 2 ≠ 10% total. It's (1.05)^2 - 1 = 10.25%.

points.label: Long-term impact
points.text: 5% inflation looks small yearly but compounds to 63% loss of purchasing power in 10 years.

points.label: Exponential, not linear
points.text: That's why starting early to invest matters - compound growth (good) vs. compound inflation (bad).

example.problem: A shirt costs Rs.500 today. Inflation is 4% per year. (a) What will it cost in 5 years? (b) In 10 years? (c) In 20 years?

slides.inSimpleWords: Inflation compounds year after year. Small yearly rises become HUGE price jumps over decades.

slides.title: Measuring Inflation: CPI (Consumer Price Index)
slides.storyContext: Ravi wants to know: "How much is inflation this year, Nani?" Nani says, "The government tracks this using something called CPI - Consumer Price Index. It checks prices of 460 items - rice, milk, fuel, electricity, school fees, transport. If CPI goes up 6%, it means ON AVERAGE, things cost 6% more than last year." Ravi nods: "So inflation is not just samosas, it's everything?"

points.label: CPI definition
points.text: Consumer Price Index measures the average price change of a basket of everyday goods and services a typical family buys.

points.label: Items tracked
points.text: Food, housing, fuel, transportation, healthcare, education, entertainment - 460 items tracked in India.

points.label: Inflation rate
points.text: If CPI was 100 last year and 106 this year, inflation is 6%. On average, things cost 6% more.

example.problem: A family's monthly basket cost Rs.10,000 last year. This year the same basket costs Rs.10,600. What is the inflation rate?

slides.inSimpleWords: CPI is like a report card for prices. It tells us how much more expensive things have gotten on average.

image.alt: Measuring Inflation: CPI (Consumer Price Index) — Inflation - Why Prices Rise Over Time

slides.title: Ravi Reads the News: RBI Raises Rates
slides.storyContext: Ravi sees a news headline: "RBI Raises Interest Rates by 0.5% to Control Inflation." He asks Nani: "What does that mean?" Nani explains: "The Reserve Bank controls how easy it is for people to borrow. When inflation gets too high, they make borrowing more expensive - high interest rates. This makes people spend less because loans cost more. Less spending means less demand, so prices cool down."

slides.title: CPI Calculation Worked Example
slides.storyContext: Mr. Patel shows Ravi how he calculates inflation for his shop basket. "This year I bought rice, oil, sugar, spices, soap, salt - 6 items. Last year: Rs.500 total. This year: Rs.575 total." Ravi calculates: (575-500)/500 = 0.15 = 15%. "Wow, 15% inflation for my favorite items!" Mr. Patel nods: "Exactly. For some families buying these daily, that's a big hit."

points.label: Basket approach
points.text: Pick your regular items, track their cost each year, calculate percentage change.

points.label: Personal inflation
points.text: Your inflation (based on what YOU buy) might differ from national average (based on all Indians).

example.problem: Your school uniform: shirt Rs.200, pants Rs.300 (last year). This year: shirt Rs.230, pants Rs.345. Inflation for your uniform?
example.solution: Last year total: Rs.500. This year: Rs.575. Inflation = (575-500)/500 x 100 = 15%.

slides.inSimpleWords: To find inflation for your stuff, add up what you spent last year vs. this year, then calculate the percentage increase.

image.alt: CPI Calculation Worked Example — Inflation - Why Prices Rise Over Time

slides.title: Inflation Over Years: A Real Rs. Example
slides.storyContext: Ravi pulls out his notebook and asks, "Nani, show me with real numbers." Nani smiles and writes: "Let's say you have Rs.1,000. In 2015, you could buy 50 textbooks at Rs.20 each. Today a textbook costs Rs.50. So Rs.1,000 now buys only 20 textbooks. Your Rs.1,000 lost power." Ravi sees it now - same money, fewer books.

points.label: Purchasing power loss
points.text: Rs.1,000 in 2015 could buy 50 items at Rs.20/item. Same Rs.1,000 in 2026 buys only 20 items at Rs.50/item. Money is worth less.

points.label: Real vs nominal value
points.text: Nominal: the number written (Rs.1,000 is still Rs.1,000). Real: what it can actually buy (far less due to inflation).

points.label: Compound effect
points.text: If inflation averages 5% per year over 10 years, Rs.1,000 loses almost half its buying power.

example.problem: Rs.100 in 2016 could buy 10 kg rice. In 2026, rice costs Rs.60/kg. How much rice does Rs.100 buy now?
example.solution: Rs.100 / Rs.60/kg = 1.67 kg. Purchasing power fell from 10 kg to 1.67 kg in 10 years due to inflation.

slides.inSimpleWords: Inflation shrinks your money's power. The same notes and coins buy you less and less over years.

image.alt: Inflation Over Years: A Real Rs. Example — Inflation - Why Prices Rise Over Time

slides.title: Nani's Retirement Worry
slides.storyContext: Nani confesses to Ravi: "I'm 60 now. I saved Rs.20 lakhs for my retirement, expecting to live comfortably. But if inflation is 6% per year, in 10 years I'll be 70 and my Rs.20 lakhs will have the buying power of only Rs.11.2 lakhs in today's money. My money shrinks while I age!" Ravi is alarmed. "What can you do?" Nani smiles: "I'm investing some of it - FDs, mutual funds - to grow faster than inflation."

slides.title: How Inflation Affects Savings
slides.storyContext: Ravi says, "I have Rs.5,000 saved in my piggy bank, Nani. When I grow up, I'll use it." Nani gently explains: "If you just keep it there and inflation is 5% per year, after 10 years your Rs.5,000 will have the buying power of only Rs.3,000 today. You didn't lose the money, but it lost power." Ravi is alarmed: "So my savings shrink?"

points.label: Savings lose power
points.text: Money kept under your pillow or in a locker doesn't grow but loses purchasing power every year due to inflation.

points.label: Example: Rs.5,000 today
points.text: At 5% annual inflation: in 10 years, Rs.5,000 buys only what Rs.3,072 buys today. You 'lost' Rs.1,928 in real value.

points.label: Why this matters
points.text: If you save for your college fees, inflation means you'll need MORE money than you saved, or fees will be higher.

example.problem: You save Rs.10,000 for college fees. Inflation is 6% per year. In 5 years, what is the REAL value of your Rs.10,000?
example.solution: Real value = 10,000 / (1.06)^5 = 10,000 / 1.338 = Rs.7,473. Your Rs.10,000 has the power of only Rs.7,473 in today's money.

slides.inSimpleWords: If you just save money without growing it, inflation eats away its power over time. Your money gets weaker, not stronger.

image.alt: How Inflation Affects Savings — Inflation - Why Prices Rise Over Time

slides.title: The Piggy Bank Question
slides.storyContext: Ravi and his sister Priya compare: he keeps Rs.5,000 in a locker for 10 years. She puts Rs.5,000 in a bank account earning 4% interest. After 10 years, with 5% inflation: Ravi has Rs.5,000 nominal, but it's worth Rs.3,069 real. Priya has Rs.7,401 nominal, and it's worth Rs.4,551 real. "Brother," Priya smiles, "my Rs.5,000 is now worth 48% more in REAL terms. Yours lost power." Ravi learns a hard lesson.

image.alt: The Piggy Bank Question — Inflation - Why Prices Rise Over Time

slides.title: How to Protect Savings from Inflation
slides.storyContext: Ravi asks urgently, "So what should I do, Nani? Throw my money away?" Nani laughs: "No! You need to make your money WORK for you. Put it in a bank savings account - the bank gives you interest (maybe 3-4%), which helps fight inflation. Or invest it where it grows faster - like mutual funds or shares. Grow your money FASTER than inflation, and it stays strong."

points.label: Bank savings account
points.text: Interest rate ~3.5% per year. Your money grows slowly but safely, helping it fight 5% inflation (though you still lose a bit).

points.label: Longer-term investments
points.text: Fixed deposits (FD), mutual funds, or stocks can give 7-10%+ returns, beating inflation and growing wealth.

points.label: The key rule
points.text: Put your money where it GROWS at a rate HIGHER than inflation. Then your real wealth increases.

example.problem: You invest Rs.10,000 in a bank FD at 6% annual interest. Inflation is 5%. After 1 year, is your real wealth growing?
example.solution: Interest earned: Rs.600. You have Rs.10,600. But 5% inflation means you lost Rs.500 in purchasing power. Net real gain: Rs.100. Yes, real wealth grows because your return (6%) beats inflation (5%).

slides.inSimpleWords: Don't let your money sit idle. Put it in investments where it grows faster than inflation, so you actually become richer.

image.alt: How to Protect Savings from Inflation — Inflation - Why Prices Rise Over Time

slides.title: Good Inflation vs. Bad Inflation
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma (Ravi's teacher) explains: "Inflation isn't always bad. If inflation is 2-3% per year and wages are rising too, people can spend and save healthily. That's GOOD inflation. But if inflation jumps to 10-15% and wages don't keep up, people get poorer fast. That's BAD inflation." Ravi asks: "What's India's inflation?" "Around 5-7% recently. Neither excellent nor terrible."

points.label: Mild inflation (2-3%)
points.text: Healthy for economy. Encourages spending and investment. Money in lockers seems wasteful. Wages usually rise too.

points.label: High inflation (8%+)
points.text: Dangerous. Erodes savings fast. Wages lag prices. Poor and elderly struggle. Real interest rates turn negative.

points.label: Deflation (prices fall)
points.text: Seems good but is actually bad. People delay spending, economy shrinks, unemployment rises.

example.problem: India's inflation is 6%. Your dad's salary is Rs.50,000/month. It rises by 5%. Does his real income grow?
example.solution: Nominal: Rs.50,000 → Rs.52,500 (+5%). Real: his money's power shrinks by 6% but salary only rose 5%. Net: his real income FELL by 1%. He feels poorer even with a salary bump!

slides.inSimpleWords: Mild inflation (2-3%) is okay. High inflation (8%+) hurts. Deflation (prices falling) sounds good but wrecks the economy.

image.alt: Good Inflation vs. Bad Inflation — Inflation - Why Prices Rise Over Time

slides.title: The Central Bank's Inflation Fight
slides.storyContext: Ravi asks Nani, "Who controls inflation?" Nani explains: "The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is like the economy's doctor. When inflation gets too high, the RBI raises interest rates - banks pay more for deposits, borrowing becomes expensive, people spend less, prices cool down. When inflation is too low or negative (deflation), they lower rates to encourage spending and borrowing. It's like turning a thermostat up or down."

slides.title: Your Turn: Track Your Own Inflation
slides.storyContext: Ravi's homework: track what YOUR family spends on food each week. Write down prices now. Ask your parents what they spent a year ago. Calculate: what's the inflation for your family's food basket? Ravi finds: milk Rs.60/liter now, Rs.50 a year ago. Bread Rs.40 now, Rs.35 a year ago. Eggs Rs.8 now, Rs.6 a year ago."

example.problem: Your family's weekly food basket this year: milk Rs.60, bread Rs.40, eggs Rs.8, rice Rs.300. Last year: milk Rs.50, bread Rs.35, eggs Rs.6, rice Rs.270. What's your family's food inflation?
example.solution: This year: Rs.408. Last year: Rs.361. Inflation = (408-361)/361 x 100 = 13%. Your family's food got 13% more expensive!

slides.inSimpleWords: Keep a price diary of things your family buys. Compare to last year. That's YOUR personal inflation rate.

slides.title: Full Example: Ravi's Future Goals
slides.storyContext: Ravi tells Nani: "When I'm 22, I want to do a master's degree. It costs Rs.5 lakhs today. If I'm 12 now, I have 10 years. I save Rs.5,000 every year." Nani checks: "If you get 6% interest and inflation is 5%, your Rs.5,000/year becomes... let's count."

example.problem: Ravi saves Rs.5,000/year for 10 years at 6% interest (compounded). Inflation averages 5%. (a) How much nominal money will he have? (b) What is the real value in today's money? (c) Will he have enough for Rs.5 lakh course in 10 years?
example.solution: (a) Savings with 6% compound interest over 10 years = Rs.65,894 (using FV of annuity formula). (b) Real value = 65,894 / (1.05)^10 = Rs.50,883 in today's money. (c) He needs Rs.5 lakh in today's value. Rs.65,894 nominal / (1.05)^10 = Rs.50,883 real. The course will inflate to ~Rs.8.15 lakhs by then (5 lakhs x 1.05^10). He's short, needs to earn more or invest at higher returns.

slides.inSimpleWords: Real inflation math: nominal savings look big, but inflation shrinks their real worth. Plan for inflation when setting long-term goals.

slides.title: Real Purchasing Power Challenge
slides.storyContext: Nani challenges Ravi: "If inflation averages 6% per year, I want to know: (1) What will a Rs.100 meal today cost in 10 years? (2) How much money will I need in 10 years to buy the same Rs.100 meal today?" This makes Ravi think about future costs, not just today's prices.

example.problem: Today's meal costs Rs.100. If inflation is 6% annually for 10 years, (a) what will that meal cost? (b) If you want to buy that same meal in 10 years, how much money do you need to set aside now (at 0% interest in your locker)?
example.solution: (a) Future cost = 100 x (1.06)^10 = Rs.179.08. (b) You need to set aside Rs.179.08 now to have enough in 10 years. OR think backwards: if you have Rs.100 now, its real purchasing power in 10 years = 100 / (1.06)^10 = Rs.55.84 in today's terms.

slides.inSimpleWords: Inflation tells you: plan ahead for higher future costs, or your money won't be enough later.

slides.title: Inflation Around the World
slides.storyContext: Ravi's friend Omar tells him about Venezuela and Turkey, where inflation got so high (100%+ per year) that people's money became worthless. "In Venezuela, prices doubled every few weeks!" Omar says. "Your salary looked big in numbers but bought nothing." Nani adds: "That's called hyperinflation. India's 6% inflation is tame by comparison. But it's still why we must invest and plan."

slides.title: What You Learned: Inflation in 5 Ideas
slides.storyContext: Nani summarizes: "Ravi, remember: inflation is when prices rise over time. It happens because of too much money, higher production costs, or supply shortages. We measure it with CPI. Over years, the same Rs.100 buys less - your money loses power. Savings just sitting there shrink in real value. So invest your money smartly to beat inflation and grow real wealth."

points.label: Inflation
points.text: is a rise in the average price of goods and services over time.

points.label: Causes
points.text: are extra money supply, higher production costs, and supply shocks.

points.label: CPI
points.text: measures average price change of things a family buys (460 items in India).

points.label: Purchasing power
points.text: of money shrinks with inflation - same Rs.100 buys less.

points.label: Strategy
points.text: invest your money at returns higher than inflation to protect and grow real wealth.

slides.inSimpleWords: Inflation makes your money weaker over time. Protect it by putting money in investments that grow faster than prices rise.

title: Ravi and the Two Piggy Banks: The Power of Compound Growth
hook: Ravi and his sister Priya both have Rs.10,000. He saves it. She invests it. 20 years later, whose Rs.10,000 is worth more?

slides.title: Ravi and the Two Piggy Banks: The Power of Compound Growth

image.alt: Ravi and the Two Piggy Banks: The Power of Compound Growth — Saving vs Investing - Making Money Work

slides.title: Two Siblings, Two Choices
slides.storyContext: On Ravi and Priya's 10th birthday, their parents give each of them Rs.10,000. Ravi puts it in a locker at home "to keep it safe." Priya shows him a bank passbook: "I'm putting mine in a savings account that gives 4% interest per year." Ravi laughs: "That's just Rs.400 a year! Why bother?" Priya smiles mysteriously: "Wait 20 years, brother. You'll see."

image.alt: Two Siblings, Two Choices — Saving vs Investing - Making Money Work

slides.title: Saving: Putting Money Aside, Safely
slides.storyContext: Uncle Dev visits and explains: "Saving is when you set money aside for the future without spending it. Ravi, your Rs.10,000 in the locker is SAFE - thieves can't take what they don't find. But it's also DORMANT - it's not growing. In 20 years, you still have Rs.10,000 notes, but they won't buy as much as today because of inflation."

points.label: Definition
points.text: Saving = putting money away for future use, typically in a safe place (home, bank, locker).

points.label: Safety
points.text: Your principal (original money) is protected. No risk of loss; no one can steal it if hidden well.

points.label: The downside
points.text: Saved money doesn't grow. With inflation, it loses purchasing power over time.

example.problem: Ravi saves Rs.1,000 under his mattress for 10 years. No interest, no returns. Inflation averages 5% annually. What is the real value of his Rs.1,000 in today's money?
example.solution: Real value = 1,000 / (1.05)^10 = 1,000 / 1.629 = Rs.614. His Rs.1,000 has the purchasing power of only Rs.614 today. He lost Rs.386 in real terms.

slides.inSimpleWords: Saving means keeping money safe but not growing it. It's secure, but inflation eats its value over time.

image.alt: Saving: Putting Money Aside, Safely — Saving vs Investing - Making Money Work

slides.title: Priya Explains Her Account
slides.storyContext: Priya shows Ravi her bank passbook after one year. "Look, brother! I now have Rs.10,400. That Rs.400 is INTEREST - free money! I didn't work for it, the bank paid me because I let them use my money." Ravi is surprised. "You're saying I should give my money to a bank?" "Yes," Priya says, "but only a bank you trust. And yes, I get less interest than at a money lender, but it's SAFE and LEGAL."

image.alt: Priya Explains Her Account — Saving vs Investing - Making Money Work

slides.title: Investing: Putting Money to Work
slides.storyContext: Priya explains to Ravi: "When you invest, you put money somewhere it can GROW. My bank account gives 4% interest. That means my Rs.10,000 earns Rs.400 in year one. In year two, I get 4% interest not just on Rs.10,000, but on Rs.10,400! It keeps growing." Uncle Dev nods: "That's compound interest, Priya. Your money works for you, earning money on money."

points.label: Definition
points.text: Investing = putting money into something (bank, bonds, stocks, mutual funds) where it can grow through returns.

points.label: Returns come from
points.text: interest (banks), dividends (stocks), capital gains (price appreciation), or multiple sources.

points.label: Growth compound
points.text: You earn returns on your principal AND on previous returns. Money grows exponentially, not linearly.

example.problem: Priya invests Rs.1,000 in a bank FD at 6% annual interest, compounded yearly. How much does she have after 5 years?
example.solution: A = P(1 + r)^n = 1,000 x (1.06)^5 = 1,000 x 1.338 = Rs.1,338. She earns Rs.338 in interest over 5 years, purely from compound growth.

slides.inSimpleWords: Investing means putting money somewhere it can grow. The longer you invest, the more your money multiplies, especially with compound interest.

image.alt: Investing: Putting Money to Work — Saving vs Investing - Making Money Work

slides.title: Year 1 Comparison
slides.storyContext: After 1 year: Ravi has Rs.10,000 (locker). Priya has Rs.10,400 (4% interest). "Rs.400 difference, big deal," Ravi shrugs. But Uncle Dev shows a chart: "Wait. If inflation is 5%, Ravi's real value dropped to Rs.9,524. Priya's is Rs.9,904. Priya's already 4% ahead in real terms. Now multiply this by 20 years..."

slides.title: Simple Interest vs. Compound Interest
slides.storyContext: Uncle Dev draws a chart: "Simple interest: you earn Rs.400/year forever on Rs.10,000. That's it. Compound interest: Year 1 you earn Rs.400 (on 10k). Year 2 you earn Rs.416 (on 10.4k). Year 3, Rs.433 (on 10.816k). The interest ITSELF earns interest. That's the magic."

points.label: Simple interest
points.text: Interest earned only on principal. Rs.10,000 at 4% = Rs.400 every year, always Rs.400.

points.label: Compound interest
points.text: Interest earned on principal AND previous interest. Rs.10,000 at 4% = Rs.400 year 1, Rs.416 year 2, Rs.433 year 3...

points.label: The difference explodes over time
points.text: 20 years at 4%: simple = Rs.10,000 + (400 x 20) = Rs.18,000. Compound = Rs.10,000 x (1.04)^20 = Rs.21,911. Compound wins by Rs.3,911!

example.problem: Rs.5,000 at 5% for 10 years: (a) simple interest total, (b) compound interest total.
example.solution: (a) Simple = 5,000 + (250 x 10) = Rs.7,500. (b) Compound = 5,000 x (1.05)^10 = Rs.8,144. Compound is Rs.644 more!

slides.inSimpleWords: Simple interest = steady extra money each year. Compound interest = growing extra money each year. Compound wins big time.

slides.title: Year 5 Checkpoint
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Priya check in after 5 years. Ravi has Rs.10,000 nominal (worth Rs.7,835 real due to 5% inflation). Priya has Rs.12,167 nominal (at 4% compound interest). "Hmm, Ravi's real value is Rs.10,000 / (1.05)^5 = Rs.7,835. Priya's real value is Rs.12,167 / (1.05)^5 = Rs.9,531. Priya's ahead, even accounting for inflation!" Uncle Dev notes this early advantage.

image.alt: Year 5 Checkpoint — Saving vs Investing - Making Money Work

slides.title: Compound Interest: The Eighth Wonder of the World
slides.storyContext: Uncle Dev pulls out a chart: "Albert Einstein called compound interest the eighth wonder of the world. Look: Priya's Rs.10,000 at 7% per year." He shows: Year 1: Rs.10,700. Year 5: Rs.14,026. Year 10: Rs.19,672. Year 20: Rs.38,697. "That Rs.10,000 nearly FOUR-TUPLES in 20 years!" Ravi's eyes widen. His Rs.10,000 in the locker is still Rs.10,000, but worth only Rs.3,769 in real value. Priya's is Rs.38,697 nominal and Rs.14,769 real!

points.label: Formula
points.text: A = P(1 + r)^n where A = final amount, P = principal, r = annual rate, n = years.

points.label: Exponential growth
points.text: Early years see small gains. Later years explode with growth. Starting early amplifies the effect.

points.label: Time is your friend
points.text: 20 years gives you 3.8x growth at 7%. But 30 years gives 7.6x. Time is MORE powerful than rate.

example.problem: You invest Rs.5,000 at 8% per year. Compare: (a) 10 years, (b) 20 years, (c) 30 years.

slides.inSimpleWords: Compound interest is like a snowball rolling down a mountain - it gets bigger and bigger as it rolls, faster and faster.

slides.title: Compound Interest Step-by-Step
slides.storyContext: Uncle Dev shows Ravi and Priya a year-by-year breakdown: Year 0: Rs.10,000. Year 1: Rs.10,000 x 1.07 = Rs.10,700. Year 2: Rs.10,700 x 1.07 = Rs.11,449. Year 3: Rs.11,449 x 1.07 = Rs.12,250. "See? Each year, you earn 7% on BOTH your original Rs.10,000 AND the interest you accumulated. That's the power."

points.label: Iteration
points.text: Year 1: earn interest on Rs.10,000. Year 2: earn interest on Rs.10,700 (original + earned). Cycle repeats.

points.label: Acceleration
points.text: Interest amount grows each year (Rs.700, then Rs.749, then Rs.801). That's exponential.

example.problem: Rs.1,000 at 10% per year, 4 years. Calculate year by year.

slides.inSimpleWords: Compound interest means you earn interest on your interest. Each year, the interest amount itself grows.

slides.title: Time Horizon and Investment Choice
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma teaches: "Your age and goals matter. If you're 15 with a 30-year horizon to retirement, you can handle 80% stocks, 20% bonds - you'll recover from crashes. If you're 60 and retiring soon, maybe 30% stocks, 70% bonds - safety matters more than growth. Match your investment risk to your TIME."

points.label: Young (15-30)
points.text: Aggressive: 80% growth assets (stocks), 20% safe (bonds/FD). Time smooths crashes.

points.label: Middle age (30-50)
points.text: Balanced: 60% growth, 40% safe. Balance risk and returns.

points.label: Near retirement (50-65)
points.text: Conservative: 30% growth, 70% safe. Protect your accumulated wealth.

example.problem: You're 20, saving for retirement at 60 (40-year horizon). Aggressive: 80% at 10% (stocks), 20% at 4% (bonds). Conservative: 40% at 10%, 60% at 4%. Calculate 40-year outcomes.
example.solution: Aggressive: 80k x 1.10^40 + 20k x 1.04^40 = 36,259k + 96k = Rs.36,355k. Conservative: 40k x 1.10^40 + 60k x 1.04^40 = 18,129k + 288k = Rs.18,417k. Aggressive grows nearly 2x more.

slides.inSimpleWords: Young investors can take more risk (stocks). Older investors need safety (bonds). Time horizon is KEY to asset allocation.

slides.title: The Power of Starting Young
slides.storyContext: Uncle Dev tells them: "Imagine three investors. Avik starts at 15, invests Rs.5,000/year for 10 years, then stops (Rs.50,000 total invested at 8%/year). Bhavna starts at 25, invests Rs.5,000/year for 30 years (Rs.1.5 lakhs total). By age 65: Avik has Rs.11.24 lakhs, Bhavna has Rs.3.37 lakhs. Same amount per year, but Avik invested LESS and has MORE because he started early. Time is magic."

slides.title: Risk vs. Return: The Investor's Trade-off
slides.storyContext: Uncle Dev explains: "Here's the catch: safety and growth don't come together for free. Bank FDs at 6%? Very safe, low risk, low return. Stocks at maybe 12% average? More risk - prices go up AND down. But over 20 years, the ups and downs average out, and you earn more." Ravi asks: "So if I want to grow money faster, I must risk losing it?" Uncle Dev: "Not lose - but you must accept that SHORT-TERM, the value might dip. LONG-TERM, stocks beat inflation by miles."

points.label: Safe = slow
points.text: Bank savings (3-4% interest) is safe but slow. Your real wealth barely beats inflation.

points.label: Growth = risk
points.text: Stocks, mutual funds (8-12% potential) can grow faster but fluctuate. Prices rise and fall.

points.label: Time reduces risk
points.text: Investing for 20+ years smooths out short-term bumps. Long-term stock investors usually win.

example.problem: Two investments: (a) Bank FD at 5%, guaranteed. (b) Mutual fund averaging 9%, with +/- 3% annual swings. Which is "better" for a 20-year goal?
example.solution: (a) Rs.10,000 at 5% for 20 years = Rs.26,533 nominal. (b) Rs.10,000 at 9% for 20 years = Rs.55,604 nominal (ignoring swings). For a 20-year goal, (b) roughly doubles (a), despite volatility. Time smooths the swings.

slides.inSimpleWords: Safer investments grow slowly. Riskier ones grow fast but wobble. If you have time (20+ years), the wobbles matter less.

image.alt: Risk vs. Return: The Investor's Trade-off — Saving vs Investing - Making Money Work

slides.title: The Emergency Fund First Rule
slides.storyContext: Uncle Dev emphasizes: "Before investing a single rupee in growth, keep 3-6 months of money in a bank account. This is your safety net for job loss, medical emergencies, or unexpected costs. Only AFTER your emergency fund is solid, invest the rest aggressively. This two-tier strategy lets you sleep at night."

slides.title: Types of Investments for Teens
slides.storyContext: Priya asks Uncle Dev: "What can I invest in at my age?" He lists: "Bank Savings Account or Fixed Deposit - safest, 4-6% return. Mutual Funds - companies pool money and invest, average 8-10%. Stocks (with parental help) - own a piece of companies, 10-15% average but bumpy. Gold - a store of value, 5-7% average. Start with FDs or mutual funds. As you learn, explore stocks."

points.label: Bank accounts
points.text: Safest, liquid (instant access), 3-4% return, no tax before 40k/year.

points.label: Fixed Deposits (FD)
points.text: Lock money for 1-5 years, guaranteed 5-6.5% return, safe.

points.label: Mutual funds
points.text: Professional fund managers invest your money in stocks/bonds, average 8-10%, moderate risk, high reward.

points.label: Stocks (Equity)
points.text: Own a share of a company, vote in decisions, earn dividends, high growth (10-15%) but risky short-term.

example.problem: Priya has Rs.20,000 to invest for 15 years. Compare: (a) FD at 6%, (b) Mutual fund at 9%. Which grows more?
example.solution: (a) FD: 20,000 x (1.06)^15 = Rs.47,931. (b) MF: 20,000 x (1.09)^15 = Rs.72,800. Mutual fund grows 52% more over 15 years, showing the power of higher returns over time.

slides.inSimpleWords: You can invest in bank accounts (safest, slowest), mutual funds (medium risk, good growth), or stocks (risky, highest growth). Choose based on your time frame.

image.alt: Types of Investments for Teens — Saving vs Investing - Making Money Work

slides.title: Interest Rate Comparison
slides.storyContext: Ravi asks: "If rates matter so much, what's the difference between 5%, 7%, and 10% over 20 years?" Uncle Dev calculates for Rs.10,000 starting amount. At 5%: Rs.26,533. At 7%: Rs.38,697. At 10%: Rs.67,275. Ravi's jaw drops: "3% difference becomes Rs.40,742 more?" Yes - that's why higher returns matter so much over long periods.

example.problem: Rs.10,000 invested for 20 years at different rates: (a) 5%, (b) 7%, (c) 10%. Calculate each and compare.

slides.inSimpleWords: Even small differences in interest rates compound into huge differences over decades. Choose higher-return investments wisely.

slides.title: Uncle Dev's Investment Philosophy
slides.storyContext: Uncle Dev tells Ravi and Priya: "I've been investing for 30 years. Early on, I was scared - stock prices went up 20%, then down 15%. But I didn't panic-sell. I kept buying more when prices dropped - got better value. Over 30 years, my Rs.50,000 initial investment became Rs.15 lakhs. Time and patience beat timing the market."

slides.title: Saving AND Investing: A Balanced Approach
slides.storyContext: By year 20, Ravi realizes his mistake. His Rs.10,000 is now only worth Rs.3,769 in real terms. Priya's is Rs.38,697 nominal, about Rs.14,769 in real value - almost 4x more! Uncle Dev says: "The ideal strategy? Keep 3-6 months of expenses as SAVINGS (emergency fund, safe). Put the rest into INVESTMENTS that beat inflation. Savings is your safety net; investing is your wealth builder."

points.label: Emergency savings
points.text: Keep 3-6 months of living expenses in a bank account - liquid, safe, for unexpected events.

points.label: Invest the rest
points.text: After emergency fund, put money into FDs, mutual funds, stocks - things that beat inflation and grow.

points.label: Time = best friend
points.text: Start investing at 15, and by 50 you'll be wealthy. Start at 25, and you'll be okay. Start at 35, and it's a struggle.

example.problem: A family needs Rs.1,50,000 for emergencies (3 months expenses). They have Rs.5,00,000 total savings. Strategy: save Rs.1,50,000 at 4% (safe), invest Rs.3,50,000 at 8% (growth) for 20 years. What do they have?
example.solution: Safe savings: 1,50,000 x (1.04)^20 = Rs.3,30,195. Investments: 3,50,000 x (1.08)^20 = Rs.16,31,934. Total = Rs.19,62,129 (vs Rs.5,00,000 today). That's nearly 4x growth by balancing safety and returns.

slides.inSimpleWords: Save for emergencies (stay safe), invest for wealth (beat inflation and grow rich). Do both.

image.alt: Saving AND Investing: A Balanced Approach — Saving vs Investing - Making Money Work

slides.title: Your Portfolio Challenge
slides.storyContext: Uncle Dev gives Ravi homework: "You have Rs.30,000. Create a split: X amount in safe bank (emergency), Y amount in mutual funds (growth). Assume 4% on savings, 9% on mutual funds, 5% inflation. In 10 years, which choice wins: 100% savings or your split?"

example.problem: Rs.30,000: Option A - all in bank at 4%. Option B - Rs.10,000 in bank (4%), Rs.20,000 in mutual fund (9%). Compare real value after 10 years (5% inflation).
example.solution: Option A: 30,000 x (1.04)^10 = Rs.44,361 nominal = Rs.34,633 real. Option B: 10k x 1.04^10 + 20k x 1.09^10 = Rs.14,802 + Rs.47,365 = Rs.62,167 nominal = Rs.48,540 real. Option B wins by Rs.13,907 real!

slides.inSimpleWords: A smart mix of safe and growth investments beats either extreme. Balance protects you AND makes you rich.

image.alt: Your Portfolio Challenge — Saving vs Investing - Making Money Work

slides.title: Full Example: Ravi's 20-Year Regret
slides.storyContext: On their 30th birthday, Ravi and Priya look back. Ravi with his locker Rs.10,000 (now worth Rs.3,769 real). Priya with her invested Rs.10,000 (now Rs.38,697 nominal, Rs.14,769 real). Uncle Dev says: "Priya's wealth grew 4x nominal, 3.9x real, while Ravi's shrunk in real terms. If they had BOTH invested instead, Ravi would have Rs.38,697 too, and Priya could have had even more with a riskier mix."

example.problem: Ravi (saver) has Rs.10,000 static for 20 years. Priya (investor) has Rs.10,000 at 7% compounded yearly. Inflation is 5% per year. (a) What is Ravi's real value after 20 years? (b) What is Priya's nominal value? (c) What is Priya's real value? (d) Who is richer in REAL terms?
example.solution: (a) Ravi's real value = 10,000 / (1.05)^20 = 10,000 / 2.653 = Rs.3,769. (b) Priya's nominal = 10,000 x (1.07)^20 = Rs.38,697. (c) Priya's real = 38,697 / (1.05)^20 = Rs.14,580. (d) Priya is 3.9x richer in real terms (Rs.14,580 vs. Rs.3,769). Investing beats saving by miles!

slides.inSimpleWords: Same Rs.10,000 with saving: stays flat but loses power. Same Rs.10,000 with investing: nearly 4-tuples, beating inflation easily.

image.alt: Full Example: Ravi's 20-Year Regret — Saving vs Investing - Making Money Work

slides.title: Your Challenge: Design Your 20-Year Portfolio
slides.storyContext: Imagine you're 15 now. You have Rs.50,000 and want to be rich by 35. Uncle Dev challenges: "Split your money: how much safe (bank, FD) and how much growth (mutual funds, stocks)? Calculate: if safe earns 5%, growth earns 10%, what will you have in 20 years?"

example.problem: You have Rs.50,000. You decide: Rs.20,000 in FD (5% return), Rs.30,000 in mutual fund (10% return), 20 years. How much do you have? What if you had put all in the mutual fund?
example.solution: Strategy mix: FD: 20,000 x (1.05)^20 = Rs.53,066. MF: 30,000 x (1.10)^20 = Rs.2,01,824. Total = Rs.2,54,890. All in MF: 50,000 x (1.10)^20 = Rs.3,36,375. The riskier all-MF strategy earns 32% more, but you had safety with FD. Your choice reflects your comfort with risk.

slides.title: Real vs Nominal Returns
slides.storyContext: Ravi asks Priya: 'You earned 7% but inflation is 5%. Did you really get 7% richer?' Priya calculates: 'No! Real return = (1.07)/(1.05) - 1 = 1.9%. Inflation ate most of my gains. That's why we must invest at rates ABOVE inflation to actually get richer.' Uncle Dev nods: 'This is why bank interest (4%) barely beats inflation (5%). You're working hard but not actually gaining much wealth.'

points.label: Nominal return
points.text: The percentage your money grew: 7% per year.

points.label: Real return
points.text: Growth after inflation: only 1.9% per year if inflation is 5%.

points.label: The gap
points.text: If you don't beat inflation with returns, you're not actually getting richer - you're losing purchasing power.

example.problem: You invest Rs.10,000 at 6% for 10 years. Inflation averages 5%. Nominal final value?Real value?
example.solution: Nominal: 10k x 1.06^10 = Rs.17,908. Real: 17,908 / 1.05^10 = Rs.10,967. You nominally gained 79%, but really gained only 10%! Inflation stole 69% of your gains.

slides.inSimpleWords: After inflation, your real gains are much smaller. Always invest above inflation to truly build wealth.

slides.title: Priya's 20-Year Reality Check
slides.storyContext: Priya looks at her 20-year projection. 'Nominal I'll have 4x. But real value after inflation? Only 1.5x.' She realizes: 'Investing beats saving, but real wealth building takes long time AND beating inflation. That's why starting YOUNG matters so much. Every year counts.'

slides.title: Inflation-Adjusted Goal Setting
slides.storyContext: Uncle Dev challenges them: 'College will cost Rs.25 lakhs in TODAY's money when you're 22. If inflation is 5%, how much will it ACTUALLY cost in 10 years? How much do you need to save/invest NOW to cover it?'

example.problem: College: Rs.25 lakh today. Inflation 5% per year. In 10 years, nominal cost? If you invest at 8%, how much do you need NOW?
example.solution: Nominal future cost = 25 lakh x 1.05^10 = Rs.40.72 lakh. To have Rs.40.72 lakh in 10 years at 8% return: need NOW = 40.72 lakh / 1.08^10 = Rs.18.82 lakh. Start investing Rs.18.82 lakh today OR Rs.1,900/month for 10 years at 8%.

slides.inSimpleWords: Plan for inflation when setting long-term goals. Future costs are MUCH higher than today. Calculate backwards from future needs.

slides.title: Automatic Investing: SIPs (Systematic Investment Plans)
slides.storyContext: Priya sets up a Systematic Investment Plan (SIP): every month, Rs.5,000 automatically deducted from her bank and invested in a mutual fund. 'I don't think about it. It just happens. And when prices are low (market down), I buy more units. When prices are high, I buy fewer units. Average cost is lower than if I tried to time it!' This takes emotion out of investing.

points.label: What is SIP
points.text: Automatic monthly investment in mutual funds. Money deducted and invested every month.

points.label: Averaging effect
points.text: Buy more units when price is low, fewer when high. Average cost per unit reduces over time.

points.label: Discipline
points.text: No emotions, no timing, no decisions needed. Just let it run for years.

example.problem: Rs.5,000/month SIP for 20 years in a mutual fund averaging 10% annual return. How much do you have?
example.solution: FV of SIP annuity = Rs.5,000 x [((1.10^20 - 1) / 0.10) / 1.10] = ~Rs.22.87 lakh total. You invested only Rs.12 lakh but have Rs.23 lakh. The 10.87 lakh gain came from compound growth!

slides.inSimpleWords: SIPs automate investing. Set it and forget it. Regular small amounts compound into big wealth over years. Best for busy people.

slides.title: Saving vs. Investing: The Bottom Line
slides.storyContext: Priya tells Ravi: "Brother, remember our piggy banks? Saving kept your money safe but weak. Investing made mine strong and rich. The lesson: saving is for emergencies, investing is for wealth. Start investing early - time is your superpower. Compound interest turns small money into big money. That's the real magic."

points.label: Saving
points.text: is keeping money safe; it protects you but doesn't grow - inflation eats it.

points.label: Investing
points.text: is putting money to work; it grows through compound interest, beating inflation.

points.label: Compound interest
points.text: is exponential growth - money earns money on money, faster over time.

points.label: Risk-return trade-off
points.text: higher returns require taking some risk, but long time frames (20+ years) smooth bumps.

points.label: Start early
points.text: is the biggest advantage; even small amounts compound into wealth over decades.

slides.inSimpleWords: Save for emergencies. Invest for wealth. The earlier and longer you invest, the richer you become. Compound interest is your best friend.

image.alt: Saving vs. Investing: The Bottom Line — Saving vs Investing - Making Money Work

subject: Financial Literacy
chapter: What is the Stock Market? Owning a Piece of a Company
title: How Priya Owns a Piece of Amazon: Understanding Stocks and the Stock Market
hook: When you buy a stock, you own a real piece of a company. Priya bought 1 share of her favorite company and became a co-owner. How does that work?

slides.title: How Priya Owns a Piece of Amazon: Understanding Stocks and the Stock Market

image.alt: How Priya Owns a Piece of Amazon: Understanding Stocks and the Stock Market — What is the Stock Market? Owning a Piece of a Company

slides.title: The Day Priya Became a Co-Owner
slides.storyContext: Priya shows Rahul her demat account (digital stocks account) on her phone. "Look, I own 2 shares of Reliance Industries," she says proudly. "So you own the company?" Rahul asks. "No, but I own a tiny piece of it!" Priya explains. "Reliance has 2.5 billion shares. I own 2. That means I'm 2 / 2,500,000,000 = 0.00000008% of the company! When Reliance makes profit, a tiny bit is mine. If the company does well, my shares become worth more."

image.alt: The Day Priya Became a Co-Owner — What is the Stock Market? Owning a Piece of a Company

slides.title: What Is a Share (Stock)?
slides.storyContext: In class, Mrs. Sharma explains using a pizza analogy: "Imagine you and your friends want to start a pizza shop. It costs Rs.1,00,000. You cut it into 100 equal pieces - each piece costs Rs.1,000. Each piece is a SHARE. If someone buys 25 pieces, they own 25% of the shop and get 25% of profits." Rahul asks, "Can you sell your shares?" "Yes! You bought at Rs.1,000/piece, but if the shop thrives, each piece is now worth Rs.2,000. You can sell for Rs.50,000 (25 pieces x Rs.2,000)."

points.label: Share definition
points.text: A share (or stock) is one equal piece of ownership in a company. If a company has 100 shares, each share = 1/100th of the company.

points.label: Ownership and profits
points.text: Shareholders (people who own shares) own pieces of the company and receive a share of profits (dividends).

points.label: Equity
points.text: Shares are called "equity" because they represent ownership. You buy equity to own a piece, not a loan.

example.problem: TechStart company issues 50,000 shares. It earns Rs.50 lakh profit this year. It decides to distribute 50% as dividends. If you own 100 shares, how much dividend do you get?
example.solution: Total dividend pool = 50,00,000 x 0.5 = Rs.25,00,000. Per share dividend = 25,00,000 / 50,000 = Rs.50/share. Your dividend = 100 shares x Rs.50 = Rs.5,000.

slides.inSimpleWords: A share is one piece of a company. Own shares, own a piece. Companies make profit, shareholders get a cut.

image.alt: What Is a Share (Stock)? — What is the Stock Market? Owning a Piece of a Company

slides.title: Why Companies Issue Shares
slides.storyContext: Rahul asks Priya: "Why would a company sell pieces of itself?" Priya explains: "Companies grow. Reliance started small, then needed money to build refineries, pipelines, gas stations. They didn't want to borrow from banks. So they sold shares. By selling 2.5 billion shares, they raised BILLIONS of rupees. Now millions of Indians own a tiny piece and benefit from growth."

image.alt: Why Companies Issue Shares — What is the Stock Market? Owning a Piece of a Company

slides.title: How Stock Prices Change
slides.storyContext: Priya watches her Reliance shares on her demat app. Today they're Rs.2,800/share. Last month Rs.2,600. "Why did they go up?" Rahul asks. Mrs. Sharma explains: "Stock price is like a bidding war. If everyone thinks Reliance will do great, they BUY shares - demand goes up, price goes UP. If bad news comes, people SELL - supply goes up, price goes DOWN. It's supply and demand."

points.label: Price determinants
points.text: Stock price rises when people want to buy (demand up, supply down). Price falls when people want to sell (supply up, demand down).

points.label: Why people buy/sell
points.text: Good earnings reports, product launches, regulatory wins = buy signals. Losses, scandals, bad news = sell signals.

points.label: Market sentiment
points.text: Sometimes prices move on emotion (hype, fear), not just facts. Irrational exuberance or panic selling happen.

example.problem: A pharma company (PharmaX) announces it discovered a cure for a disease. Its stock jumps from Rs.500 to Rs.750 in one week. You own 10 shares. What is your gain?
example.solution: Purchase value = 10 x Rs.500 = Rs.5,000. Current value = 10 x Rs.750 = Rs.7,500. Gain = Rs.2,500 (50% profit in a week!). This is capital appreciation from good news.

slides.inSimpleWords: Stock prices go up when people want to buy, down when people want to sell. Good news = more buyers. Bad news = more sellers.

image.alt: How Stock Prices Change — What is the Stock Market? Owning a Piece of a Company

slides.title: A Stock Price Crash
slides.storyContext: Rahul sees his favorite tech company's stock dropped 30% after missing profit targets. "Should I sell now and get out?" he panics. Mrs. Sharma explains: "This is normal. Good companies have bad quarters. If you believe in the company long-term and still think it's solid, hold. If you panic-sell after a 30% drop, you lock in losses. If you had held, it likely recovers in 6-12 months. Time heals stock wounds."

slides.title: Market Sentiment and Herd Behavior
slides.storyContext: Priya learns from watching markets: "Sometimes prices move on pure emotion. Everyone wants to buy Tesla, so prices zoom up even if earnings are flat. This is herd behavior - people copy others without thinking. Then bad news triggers panic selling. The stock crashes not because the company is worse, but because sentiment flipped."

points.label: Bull market
points.text: Everyone is optimistic, buying stocks, prices go up. Positive sentiment dominates.

points.label: Bear market
points.text: Everyone is pessimistic, selling stocks, prices fall. Negative sentiment dominates.

points.label: Contrary investing
points.text: Buy when sentiment is fearful (prices low), sell when sentiment is euphoric (prices high). Buy the dip!

example.problem: Stock X is solid (earnings +10%). But everyone pessimistic, X falls 20% in a week. Rational?
example.solution: No! Company improved but price fell. This is herd panic. Brave investors buy at 20% discount. When sentiment reverses, they profit.

slides.inSimpleWords: Herd behavior causes irrational price swings. Fear crashes prices, greed pumps them. Use emotion to your advantage.

slides.title: Supply and Demand in Stock Markets
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma draws on the board: "Imagine TechCorp stock. Only 100 shares exist. If 50 people want to buy but only 5 people want to sell, what happens? The 50 buyers compete - they bid higher prices. The price climbs! Reverse it: 5 people want to buy, 50 want to sell. Price falls as sellers panic-drop prices." Priya sees it now: stocks are just auctions."

points.label: More buyers than sellers
points.text: Prices rise. Buyers bid higher to compete for limited shares.

points.label: More sellers than buyers
points.text: Prices fall. Sellers lower prices to entice buyers.

points.label: Perfect balance
points.text: Prices stabilize. The equilibrium price is where demand = supply.

example.problem: Stock X has 1,000 shares. At Rs.100/share: 200 people want to buy, 50 want to sell. What happens to price?
example.solution: 4x more buyers than sellers. Buyers compete by bidding higher (Rs.105, Rs.110, etc.). Price rises until it reaches a point where demand = supply (maybe Rs.120 - some buyers drop out, some sellers enter).

slides.inSimpleWords: Stock prices are auctions. More buyers = price up. More sellers = price down. Simple market forces.

slides.title: The Stock Market and Exchanges (NSE, BSE)
slides.storyContext: Priya tells Rahul: "India has two main stock exchanges: NSE (National Stock Exchange) in Mumbai and BSE (Bombay Stock Exchange), also Mumbai. They're like giant bazaars where people buy and sell shares ALL DAY. Whenever you buy a share, you're buying from someone who sold it. The exchange matches buyers and sellers, sets the price." Rahul: "So I don't buy from the company itself?" "Right! You buy from other investors in the market."

points.label: Stock exchange
points.text: A marketplace where shares are bought and sold. India has NSE and BSE; the US has NYSE and NASDAQ.

points.label: Listings
points.text: Companies "list" on an exchange to let public buy/sell their shares. Before that, only founders/investors own.

points.label: Trading
points.text: Every day, millions of shares change hands. Prices update every second based on buy/sell orders.

points.label: Indices
points.text: Sensex (BSE top 30 companies) and Nifty50 (NSE top 50) track overall market health.

example.problem: You place an order to BUY 5 shares of TCS at Rs.3,500/share on NSE. Within seconds, your order is matched with someone SELLING 5 shares at that price. You now own 5 TCS shares. What did you pay?
example.solution: 5 shares x Rs.3,500/share = Rs.17,500 (plus small fees). You are now part-owner of Tata Consultancy Services, one of India's biggest IT companies.

slides.inSimpleWords: Stock exchanges (NSE, BSE) are markets where millions of investors buy and sell shares daily. Your broker connects you to these markets.

slides.title: Opening a Demat Account
slides.storyContext: Rahul wants to start investing but is confused. "How do I buy shares?" he asks. Priya walks him through: "First, open a bank account if you don't have one. Second, open a demat account with a broker - I use Zerodha, it's online and free. Third, link your bank to your demat account. Fourth, download their app, search for a company, click BUY, enter how many shares - done! Your shares appear in your account." Rahul: "That's it?" "Basically yes. Then you watch prices, maybe sell someday, or hold forever."

slides.title: Reading Earnings Reports
slides.storyContext: Priya decides to read Reliance's quarterly earnings report before buying. She checks: revenue, profit, cash flow, debt, and margins. If revenue is up 15% but profit only up 5%, that means costs are rising faster than sales. Red flag. She learns smart investing means understanding HOW companies make money.

slides.title: Demat Account and Trading
slides.storyContext: Rahul asks, "How do you actually hold your shares?" Priya shows him: "I have a demat account with my broker - it's like a digital locker. My shares live there. When I want to buy, I place an order through my broker's app (like Zerodha, Angel Broking, ICICI Direct). The broker buys for me, puts shares in my demat account. When I sell, it removes them." Mrs. Sharma adds: "No physical certificates anymore - everything is digital."

points.label: Demat account
points.text: Short for "dematerialized." A digital account that holds your shares electronically.

points.label: Broker
points.text: An intermediary (Zerodha, Angel, ICICI Direct) that connects you to the exchange. You pay them commission (Rs.20-50 per trade).

points.label: Process
points.text: Open demat account -> link a bank -> place buy/sell orders via broker's app -> funds transfer automatically.

example.problem: You open a demat account with Rs.50,000 in your bank. You buy 10 shares of HDFC Bank at Rs.1,500/share. Broker charges Rs.50 commission. How much is deducted from your bank account?
example.solution: Share cost = 10 x Rs.1,500 = Rs.15,000. Commission = Rs.50. Total debit = Rs.15,050. Your bank shows -Rs.15,050, demat account shows +10 HDFC shares.

slides.inSimpleWords: A demat account is a digital locker for your shares. A broker is the middleman who executes your buy/sell orders for a small fee.

slides.title: Priya's First Trade
slides.storyContext: Priya describes her first stock purchase: "I researched Reliance for a week - read earnings reports, industry news, analyst recommendations. Then I opened Zerodha, searched 'Reliance,' saw the current price Rs.2,550/share, entered 2 shares, clicked BUY. My bank auto-deducted Rs.5,100 + Rs.20 commission. In minutes, my demat account showed 2 Reliance shares. I was a shareholder! My heart raced for weeks checking the price." Rahul smiles: "Did you make money?" "I'm up Rs.500 so far. But I'm holding long-term - 5 years at least."

slides.title: Dividends: Getting Paid as a Shareholder
slides.storyContext: Priya receives a surprise: Rs.500 dividend into her bank account from her Reliance shares! She explains to Rahul: "When a company earns profit, it can either reinvest it OR pay shareholders a piece as dividend. Reliance declared 10% dividend. My 2 shares earned Rs.250 each. I got Rs.500!" Mrs. Sharma notes: "Companies that pay dividends are often mature, stable companies like banks, oil firms, utilities."

points.label: Dividend
points.text: A share of company profits paid to shareholders, usually as cash per share (e.g., Rs.50/share).

points.label: Dividend yield
points.text: Annual dividend per share divided by share price. If share costs Rs.1,000 and dividend is Rs.50, yield is 5%.

points.label: Types
points.text: Dividends can be cash (paid to your bank) or reinvested (more shares bought automatically).

example.problem: You own 100 shares of ICICI Bank. Each share is Rs.500. The bank declares a Rs.25/share dividend. (a) How much cash do you get? (b) What is the dividend yield?
example.solution: (a) Dividend received = 100 x Rs.25 = Rs.2,500. (b) Dividend yield = (25 / 500) x 100 = 5%. You earn 5% annual return just from dividends, without selling shares.

slides.inSimpleWords: When a company makes profit and decides to share it with owners (shareholders), it pays dividends. Free money for owning shares!

image.alt: Dividends: Getting Paid as a Shareholder — What is the Stock Market? Owning a Piece of a Company

slides.title: The Dividend Timeline
slides.storyContext: Rahul asks: "How often do companies pay dividends?" Priya explains: "Usually quarterly (every 3 months) or annually (once a year). The company announces a 'dividend declaration date,' then you have to own shares by the 'record date' to get it. Then they send the money to your bank by the 'payment date.' It's like waiting for a paycheck - you own the company, so you get a cut of profits!"

slides.title: Capital Gains: Making Money from Price Appreciation
slides.storyContext: Priya bought Reliance at Rs.2,600/share six months ago. Today it's Rs.2,800. She sells 2 shares and pockets Rs.4,000 (2 x Rs.2,800) vs. her original Rs.5,200 (2 x Rs.2,600). She lost Rs.200? No! She had NO shares before, so she GAINED Rs.4,000. But had she waited to sell at Rs.2,600, she'd get Rs.5,200. The Rs.400 gain (Rs.2,800 - Rs.2,600) x 2 shares = Rs.400 CAPITAL GAIN. Mrs. Sharma explains: "Capital gain is profit from selling at a higher price than you bought."

points.label: Capital gain
points.text: Profit from selling a share at a higher price than you bought it. Example: bought at Rs.100, sold at Rs.150 = Rs.50 gain per share.

points.label: Long-term vs. short-term
points.text: Hold >1 year = long-term (taxed at 20%, more favorable). Hold <1 year = short-term (taxed at slab rates).

points.label: Tax impact
points.text: Capital gains are taxable income. If you gain Rs.10,000 in a year, you must report it in tax filing.

example.problem: You bought 50 shares of Infosys at Rs.1,200/share (total: Rs.60,000). After 2 years, you sell all at Rs.1,500/share (total: Rs.75,000). (a) What is your capital gain? (b) If long-term tax is 20%, what tax do you owe? (c) What is your net profit after tax?
example.solution: (a) Capital gain = Rs.75,000 - Rs.60,000 = Rs.15,000. (b) Tax = Rs.15,000 x 20% = Rs.3,000. (c) Net profit = Rs.15,000 - Rs.3,000 = Rs.12,000 (you keep Rs.12,000 of the gain).

slides.inSimpleWords: Capital gain is profit from selling a share at a higher price than you bought. Long-term gains (held >1 year) are taxed less generously.

slides.title: Stock Analysis Practice
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma gives the class a task: "Pick a real Indian company (Reliance, HDFC, Infosys, TCS, ICICI). Find its current stock price online. Find its dividend per share. Calculate the dividend yield. Then ask: at this price and dividend, is it attractive to invest in for 5 years?"

example.problem: Reliance stock: Rs.2,600/share today. Annual dividend: Rs.200/share. (a) Calculate dividend yield. (b) If you expect price to grow 8%/year, what's your total annual return?
example.solution: (a) Dividend yield = (200 / 2,600) x 100 = 7.69%. (b) Total return = 7.69% (dividend) + 8% (capital appreciation) = 15.69%/year average. Very attractive for a 5-year horizon!

slides.inSimpleWords: Research real stocks: dividend yield + expected price growth = your total return. Higher total return = better investment (but higher risk too).

image.alt: Stock Analysis Practice — What is the Stock Market? Owning a Piece of a Company

slides.title: Market Cycles and Valuation
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma teaches: "Stock prices cycle. When a company is hot, prices get inflated (expensive). When sentiment sours, prices crash (cheap). A good investor buys when prices are low relative to earnings (P/E ratio low), sells when they're high (P/E ratio high)."

points.label: P/E ratio
points.text: Share price divided by annual earnings per share. Low P/E = cheap, High P/E = expensive.

points.label: Buy low, sell high
points.text: Buy when P/E is low (market pessimism), sell when P/E is high (market hype). Timing is hard, but buying value is easier.

points.label: Value investing
points.text: Buy great companies when unpopular. Hold as market recognizes value. Profits come from patience, not trading speed.

example.problem: Stock A: Rs.100/share, earns Rs.10 (P/E=10). Stock B: Rs.200/share, earns Rs.10 (P/E=20). Same earnings. Which is better value?
example.solution: Stock A is cheaper (lower P/E). You pay Rs.10 per Re.1 of earnings vs Rs.20 for Stock B. Same earnings, A is better value.

slides.inSimpleWords: P/E ratio tells you if stock is cheap or expensive. Low P/E = good value. High P/E = might be overpriced. Hunt low P/E.

slides.title: Risk in Stocks: Why Prices Fall
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma warns Rahul: "Stocks are NOT always winning. If a company's revenue drops, if competitors grow stronger, if bad news breaks, stock prices FALL. Someone who bought TechStart at Rs.200/share six months ago and sold at Rs.100/share just LOST 50%!" Priya adds, "That's why they say 'stocks can go to zero.' But if you pick good companies and hold long, that risk shrinks."

points.label: Business risk
points.text: Company earns less profit or closes - share price falls. Worst case: bankruptcy, shares become worthless.

points.label: Market risk
points.text: Recession or stock market crash can drag down even healthy companies' prices.

points.label: Mitigation
points.text: Diversify (own many companies, not just one). Research before buying. Hold long-term (5-10+ years, bumps smooth out).

example.problem: You bought Tesla shares at Rs.20,000/share. Bad news crashes the price to Rs.12,000. You lose Rs.8,000 per share. If you own 2 shares, you lost Rs.16,000. Should you panic-sell?
example.solution: Depends on your investment goal and time frame. If it's short-term money, yes, panic-sell to minimize loss. If it's 10-year retirement money and Tesla is still a solid company, hold - prices usually recover. Panic-selling locks in losses; holding allows recovery.

slides.inSimpleWords: Stocks can fall when companies struggle or markets crash. Long-term holding, diversification, and careful research reduce this risk.

image.alt: Risk in Stocks: Why Prices Fall — What is the Stock Market? Owning a Piece of a Company

slides.title: Portfolio Diversification
slides.storyContext: Priya tells Rahul: "I don't put all my money in one stock. I have Reliance, HDFC Bank, TCS, and Infosys. If Reliance drops 20%, my whole portfolio doesn't crash. Maybe it drops 5%. This is called diversification." Rahul asks, "How many stocks should I own?" "As a teen, 3-5 good companies is enough. Add as you earn more."

slides.title: Full Example: Priya's Stock Portfolio Journey
slides.storyContext: Over 5 years, Priya's investment story: She invests Rs.1,00,000 total. She buys 50 shares of Reliance at Rs.2,000 (Rs.1,00,000), holds for 5 years. Reliance grows well, price rises to Rs.3,200/share. Total value: Rs.1,60,000. She also received Rs.20,000 in dividends (Rs.200/year x 5 years x 50 shares). Her total return: Rs.1,60,000 + Rs.20,000 = Rs.1,80,000 from Rs.1,00,000 invested. Net profit: Rs.80,000 (80% gain)!

example.problem: Priya invests Rs.1,00,000 in 50 Reliance shares at Rs.2,000/share today. Over 5 years: (a) price rises to Rs.3,200/share, (b) company pays Rs.200/share/year dividend. Calculate: (1) capital gain, (2) dividend income, (3) total return, (4) annualized return rate.
example.solution: (1) Capital gain = (Rs.3,200 - Rs.2,000) x 50 = Rs.60,000. (2) Dividend = Rs.200/share/year x 5 years x 50 = Rs.50,000. (3) Total return = Rs.60,000 + Rs.50,000 = Rs.1,10,000 on Rs.1,00,000 = 110% gain. (4) Annualized = ((Rs.2,10,000 / Rs.1,00,000)^(1/5) - 1) x 100 = 16.6% per year (very strong!).

slides.inSimpleWords: Smart stock investing combines capital gains (price rise) + dividend income. Over years, real wealth multiplies from compound returns.

slides.title: The Long Game
slides.storyContext: Priya reflects: "When I started 5 years ago, I checked stock prices daily. It stressed me out! Now I check maybe quarterly. My diversified portfolio is up 80% overall. The secret? I stopped trying to time the market (buy low, sell high). Instead, I buy good companies at reasonable prices and hold for 5-10 years. Time in the market beats timing the market." Mrs. Sharma nods approvingly."

slides.title: Mutual Funds: Investing Without Picking Stocks
slides.storyContext: Priya learns about mutual funds from her father: 'If picking individual stocks is hard, mutual funds do it for you. A professional fund manager buys 50-100 stocks in a mutual fund. You buy units in the fund, not individual shares. Your risk spreads across many companies, so one bad stock doesn't kill you.'

points.label: What is a mutual fund
points.text: A basket of stocks managed by professionals. You buy units; manager does the picking.

points.label: Types
points.text: Growth funds (aggressive, mostly stocks), Balanced funds (mix), Debt funds (conservative, mostly bonds).

points.label: Advantages
points.text: Instant diversification, expert management, lower fees, easy to buy via SIPs (automatic monthly investment).

example.problem: You invest Rs.500/month in a balanced mutual fund for 15 years. Average return 8%. How much do you have?
example.solution: Using future value of annuity (Rs.500/month, 8%/year): ~Rs.1,52,000 total. Your Rs.90k invested grows to 1.7x. Better than keeping money in a bank!

slides.inSimpleWords: Mutual funds let professionals pick stocks for you. Less stress, good returns, automatic diversification.

slides.title: Your Challenge: Build Your First Portfolio
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma gives the class homework: "Imagine you have Rs.50,000 to invest for 5 years. Pick 3 Indian companies (Reliance, HDFC, Infosys, TCS, ICICI, etc.). Research their business. Decide how many shares to buy at current prices. Predict: if they grow 10-15% per year, what will your portfolio be worth in 5 years?"

example.problem: You pick 3 stocks: (a) HDFC Bank, Rs.1,500/share, you buy 15 shares (Rs.22,500), expect 12% annual growth. (b) Reliance, Rs.2,500/share, you buy 6 shares (Rs.15,000), expect 10% growth. (c) TCS, Rs.3,200/share, you buy 3 shares (Rs.9,600), expect 14% growth. What is each position worth in 5 years?

slides.title: Compare: Stock vs Mutual Fund vs Bank Account
slides.storyContext: Rahul asks Priya: 'Which should I invest in?' Priya says, 'It depends on your knowledge and time. Bank account (4%, safe, boring): good for emergency funds. Mutual fund (8-10%, moderate, hands-off): good for busy people who want growth. Stocks (10-15%, risky, needs research): good if you love analyzing companies.' Rahul nods: 'Different tools for different goals!'

example.problem: You have Rs.1,00,000 for 10 years. (a) Bank account at 4%, (b) MF at 8%, (c) Stocks at 10% (your picks, researched). What do you have?
example.solution: (a) Bank: 100k x 1.04^10 = Rs.1,48,024. (b) MF: 100k x 1.08^10 = Rs.2,15,892. (c) Stocks: 100k x 1.10^10 = Rs.2,59,374. Stocks win by Rs.44k over MF, but require 10 years of research!

slides.inSimpleWords: Bank accounts are safe but slow. Mutual funds are hands-off and fast. Stocks are fastest but need homework. Pick your comfort level.

slides.title: Stocks and Stock Market: The Essentials
slides.storyContext: Priya summarizes for Rahul: "A share is a piece of a company. Own shares, own the company's future. You buy and sell on stock exchanges (NSE, BSE) via a demat account. You make money two ways: capital gains (price rises) and dividends (company profits). But prices can fall, so diversify and hold long. Start young, invest consistently, and compound returns will make you wealthy."

points.label: Share
points.text: is one piece of company ownership. Own shares, earn from profits and growth.

points.label: Stock price
points.text: moves based on supply/demand and company performance. Rises on good news, falls on bad news.

points.label: Stock market
points.text: (NSE, BSE) is where millions trade shares daily. Demat account + broker = your access.

points.label: Returns
points.text: come from capital gains (selling at profit) + dividends (company profit sharing).

points.label: Risk
points.text: exists; prices can fall. Diversify, research, hold long-term to reduce risk and profit.

slides.inSimpleWords: Stocks are ownership pieces of companies. Buy good companies cheap, hold for years, collect dividends, and watch wealth grow. Start young!
